youtube.baslik: Workplace Audiometric Monitoring and Threshold Shift | Lesson 225 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How is the hearing of workers in noisy jobs monitored? In this lesson we learn about the baseline audiogram, the conditions for periodic tests, how to calculate a standard threshold shift (STS), age correction, the NIOSH criterion and the steps taken when a shift is found.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95, Occupational Noise Exposure (including Appendix F); NIOSH (1998), Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Occupational Noise Exposure; Berger et al., The Noise Manual (AIHA); Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Regulation on the Protection of Employees from Noise-Related Risks, Türkiye (Official Gazette, 28.07.2013, No. 28721).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Baseline audiogram, STS and age correction
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about audiometric monitoring of workers in noisy jobs and why the baseline audiogram matters so much.
We will cover how to calculate a standard threshold shift, age correction and the steps taken when a shift is found.
Audiometric monitoring is not a stand-alone test but one part of a hearing conservation program.
The program starts with measurement showing who is exposed to how much noise.
Engineering controls that reduce noise at its source and along its path are the foundation of the program.
Selecting protectors, checking their fit and training workers to use them are the steps we saw in the previous lesson.
Audiometric monitoring is the early warning system that shows whether the program is really working.
All these steps are recorded, because comparisons made years later depend on these records.
Everything starts with the baseline audiogram taken at hiring; this is the person's reference audiogram.
Workers who remain exposed to noise are retested periodically, in many programs once a year.
Each new audiogram is compared with the baseline audiogram frequency by frequency.
A change that looks meaningful is confirmed with a retest before any decision is made.
A confirmed change is reported to the worker, and the protective measures are reviewed.
The aim is not to document permanent loss but to catch the change before the loss progresses.

maddeler.metin: At start of exposure, within 6 months

yan.metin: The *reference* point for all later comparisons

cumleler: OSHA, the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration, requires a baseline audiogram within six months of the start of exposure.
Before the test, the worker must be away from workplace noise for at least fourteen hours; hearing protectors can also be used to meet this.
Otherwise, a temporary threshold shift gets into the baseline values and all later comparisons are misleading.
The test is done at 500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000 and 6000 Hz, separately for each ear.

cumleler.yazi: In Türkiye, the 2013 noise regulation requires the employer to arrange hearing tests when exposure exceeds the upper action value.
cumleler.ses: In Türkiye, the twenty thirteen noise regulation requires the employer to arrange hearing tests when exposure exceeds the upper action value.

cumleler: If the risk assessment calls for it, hearing tests may also be arranged for those above the lower action value.
The interval of health surveillance is set by the occupational physician based on the risk assessment results; check the current regulation.
Year-to-year comparison is meaningful only if tests are done under the same conditions; room noise must not mask thresholds.
The audiometer should pass a daily listening check and be calibrated at regular intervals.
As far as possible, the same type of earphone and the same threshold method should be used.
Otoscopy is done before testing; impacted earwax can temporarily worsen thresholds.
Noise outside work, firearm use, medications and ear disease are asked about and recorded at every test.
Doing the periodic test at the start of a shift prevents a temporary shift from that day's noise from affecting the result.
In this example, the dashed navy line shows the baseline audiogram of a worker's right ear.
The red line is the annual audiogram of the same ear five years later.
By the OSHA definition, a standard threshold shift, or STS, looks at only three frequencies.
These frequencies are 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz, the region where noise damage appears earliest.
An average worsening of ten decibels or more at these three frequencies, relative to baseline, counts as a standard threshold shift.
Each ear is assessed separately; a shift in one ear is enough.
The values in the example are for teaching; now let us do the calculation on a table.
At 2000 Hz, the threshold has worsened from 10 to 20 decibels; the difference is 10 decibels.
At 3000 Hz, from 15 to 30 decibels; the difference is 15 decibels.
At 4000 Hz, from 20 to 35 decibels; the difference is again 15 decibels.
The three differences add up to 40, an average of about 13 decibels; this exceeds the ten decibel criterion.
So without age correction, this ear shows a standard threshold shift.
Over five years, part of the change in thresholds may come not from noise but simply from aging.
OSHA allows age correction when deciding on a standard threshold shift.
The values to use are given in tables in an appendix of the standard.
These tables are separate for women and men; the expected threshold change between the two ages is subtracted from the measured one.
If the average difference falls below ten decibels after correction, the shift does not count as a standard threshold shift.
NIOSH, the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, recommends no age correction.
This is because tables based on groups can hide noise damage in an individual.
Which approach applies depends on the regulation the program follows; the record should state clearly which one was used.

sahneler.baslik: What happens when a *shift is found?*
cumleler: Under OSHA, if an annual test shows a shift, a retest may be done within thirty days and used in place of the annual audiogram.
If the shift is confirmed, the worker is informed in writing within twenty one days.
Workers without protectors are given them; for those who have them, fit is rechecked, training repeated or a better protector chosen.
At this stage, individual fit testing can show whether the problem lies in the protector or in how it is used.
If the shift suggests a cause other than noise or an ear disease, the worker is referred to a physician.
When the shift is persistent, the baseline audiogram may be revised for later comparisons.
Because the OSHA criterion looks at an average of three frequencies, it can miss a clear change at a single frequency.

cumleler.yazi: For this reason, the 1998 NIOSH criteria document proposed a more sensitive criterion.
cumleler.ses: For this reason, the nineteen ninety eight NIOSH criteria document proposed a more sensitive criterion.

cumleler: By this criterion, a worsening of 15 decibels at any frequency from 500 to 6000 Hz, in either ear, is significant.
The change is confirmed with an immediate retest and then with a separate confirmation test.
A more sensitive criterion gives an earlier warning, but the chance of false alarms also rises slightly.
OSHA also requires a confirmed shift to be recorded as an occupational illness if the three-frequency average is 25 dB HL or more.
Noise usually affects both ears similarly; a clear, unexplained asymmetry calls for referral to a physician.
A large worsening over a short time suggests a cause other than noise.
Signs of ear disease, such as ear discharge, pain or a feeling of fullness, are also reasons for referral.
One-sided tinnitus and dizziness may call for assessment for retrocochlear causes.
An air-bone gap suggests a conductive problem other than noise.
The audiologist does not diagnose; they document the finding accurately and share it with the occupational physician and the ENT physician.
In this example, a worker's annual audiogram shows a mild notch in the right ear.
The left ear, however, has a much deeper loss in the same region; a clear difference has developed between the ears.
If the history reveals that the person uses a shotgun on weekends, this asymmetry may be explained by the ear closer to the muzzle.
But if the history gives no such explanation, the asymmetry calls for referral to a physician to rule out retrocochlear causes.
In both cases, exposure outside work is recorded, because protection advice should also cover life outside work.
The example is for teaching; determining the cause belongs to the physician's assessment.
At every test, the date, device, calibration status, tester and history are fully recorded.
The result is explained to the worker in plain language and compared with the baseline audiogram.
Seeing the change in their own audiogram is often the strongest motivation for wearing protectors.
When data from workers in the same department are reviewed together, we can tell whether the program is working there.
These records are personal health data; sharing follows the relevant regulations and principles of confidentiality.

sahneler.metin: Test at the start of the shift and ask about protector use at every test. If you see a shift, confirm it with a retest first, then decide.
cumleler: A tip from the field: if possible, do the periodic test at the start of the shift, before that day's noise exposure.
A test at the end of the shift can make a temporary threshold shift look like a permanent one.
At every test, ask about and record the protector type, wearing time and noise outside work.
When you see a shift, refit the earphones and repeat the test; do not decide on a single measurement.

maddeler.metin: OSHA and NIOSH differ on age

cumleler: The baseline audiogram is taken after at least fourteen hours without noise and is the reference for all later tests.
Under OSHA, a standard threshold shift is an average worsening of ten decibels or more at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz.
OSHA allows age correction; NIOSH recommends no correction and a 15 decibel criterion at a single frequency.
When a shift is found, it is confirmed with a retest, reported to the worker and protective measures are reviewed.

sahneler.soru: Shifts of 5, 10 and 15 dB at 2, 3 and 4 kHz: what is the OSHA result?
sahneler.aciklama: Average difference (5 + 10 + 15) / 3 = _10 dB_; the criterion is 10 dB or more.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: if thresholds at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz worsen by 5, 10 and 15 decibels, what is the result by the OSHA criterion?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: there is a standard threshold shift.
The average of the three differences is exactly ten decibels, and the criterion is ten or more; age correction may change the result.
